concepts.title: Forcing Reliable JSON: Schema-Constrained Generation
concepts.description: Asking a model to 'please respond in JSON' is just one more instruction competing with everything else in the prompt for influence over the next token; schema-constrained decoding instead physically restricts which tokens the model is even allowed to emit at each step, which is the mechanical reason it succeeds where politer prompting fails.
learningObjectives: Explain the mechanical difference between prompting a model to 'respond in JSON' and using a genuine schema-constrained decoding feature.
Describe how grammar-constrained decoding restricts the token-selection process at each generation step, in terms of the softmax mechanism from earlier modules.
Predict specific failure modes of instruction-only JSON requests and explain which ones schema constraints eliminate and which they don't.
Design a JSON schema for a structured-extraction task and use it with a provider's structured-output feature.
Explain why schema validity does not imply semantic correctness, and build defensive validation on top of constrained decoding rather than instead of it.

sections.heading: Two Different Kinds of 'Please Respond in JSON'
sections.body:
The earlier module on prompting already established that a plain-text instruction like 'return the result as JSON' is just more conditioning text -- it shifts the probability distribution toward JSON-shaped output without hard-constraining it, which is exactly why models following only that instruction still occasionally wrap output in prose, add a markdown code fence, or invent a field name that was never in your schema. Schema-constrained generation -- variously branded across providers as JSON mode, Structured Outputs, or built directly into function/tool calling -- solves the same problem through a completely different mechanism, not just a more forceful version of the same instruction.

The distinction matters enough to state precisely: an instruction changes what the model is *likely* to generate; a schema constraint changes what the model is *permitted* to generate, token by token, at the decoding step itself. Those are different kinds of guarantee, and conflating them is the single most common design mistake teams make when they first reach for structured output -- assuming that upgrading from a plain instruction to a stronger-sounding instruction ('You MUST return only valid JSON, nothing else') closes the reliability gap, when only an actual constrained-decoding feature does.

sections.heading: How Schema-Constrained Decoding Actually Works, Under the Hood
What This Guarantees, and the Sharp Edges It Doesn't Cover
sections.body:
Constrained decoding guarantees syntactic validity and structural conformance to your schema -- the output really will parse, really will have the required keys, and really will have values of the declared types. It does **not** guarantee that those values are correct. A model forced to emit an integer for a `"year_founded"` field will emit *some* syntactically valid integer even if it has no real basis for the true value -- the same hallucination mechanism from the how-LLMs-work module operates entirely underneath the constraint layer, which only ever restricts syntax, never truth.

There's a sharper, less obvious edge case worth internalizing: an **enum field forces a choice among the options you declared, even when none of them is actually correct for this specific input.** If a schema declares `"category": {"enum": ["billing", "technical", "other"]}` and the true answer is something the schema author simply didn't anticipate, the model still has to pick one of the three -- it cannot decline, cannot add a fourth option on the fly, and cannot leave the field empty unless you explicitly made it nullable. The constraint doesn't know or care whether any of its allowed values are *good* answers; it only enforces that the answer is *one of* them.

A second, subtler cost shows up specifically on harder tasks: constraining every single output token to match a rigid final schema can remove the model's room to 'think' before committing to an answer. If a schema forces the very first token of the response to already be part of the final structured answer, there's no space left for the kind of intermediate reasoning tokens that (as covered in the sampling and next-token-prediction modules) measurably improve accuracy on multi-step problems -- the model has to jump straight to a committed, schema-shaped answer with nothing to condition on but the raw question. The fix, covered in the next section, is to design the schema itself to make room for that reasoning rather than abandoning constrained decoding altogether.

sections.heading: Designing Schemas That Help Rather Than Hurt

examples.title: Instruction-Only JSON vs a Genuine Schema Constraint
examples.code:
# Instruction-only: just more conditioning text, no hard guarantee
weak_response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Extract the name and age from: 'Amy is 34.' Respond with JSON only."}],
)
# raw might be: 'Sure! Here you go:\n```json\n{"name": "Amy", "age": 34}\n```'

# Schema-constrained: the decoder cannot emit a token that breaks this shape
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}, "age": {"type": "integer"}},
    "required": ["name", "age"],
    "additionalProperties": False
}
strong_response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Extract the name and age from: 'Amy is 34.'"}],
    response_format={"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "extraction", "schema": schema, "strict": True}},
)
# raw is guaranteed to be exactly: {"name": "Amy", "age": 34}
examples.explanation: Both calls are asking for the same information, and both will very often produce usable output in casual testing -- which is precisely why the distinction is easy to underrate until it fails in production. The weak call's output has to be defensively unwrapped (stripping the markdown fence, ignoring the leading 'Sure!') before `json.loads` will even accept it, and that unwrapping logic is guessing at a pattern rather than relying on a guarantee. The strong call, using a genuine `json_schema` response format, never produces the fence or the pleasantry at all -- not because the model was told more forcefully not to, but because those tokens were never eligible for selection once the schema constraint was active. The reliability difference is structural, not a matter of degree.

examples.title: An Enum Forcing a Choice, Even the Wrong One
examples.explanation: The constraint did exactly what it promises: it produced syntactically valid JSON with a value from the declared enum, with total reliability. What it could not do is notice, on your behalf, that the enum itself was incomplete for this input -- 'billing' simply isn't an eligible token sequence here, so the model is mechanically forced into the closest available wrong answer, most likely 'support' as a plausible-sounding fallback. This is exactly the kind of failure that schema validity checks alone will never catch, since `{"department": "support"}` passes schema validation perfectly -- catching it requires either a broader enum, an explicit 'other' escape option, or downstream business-logic validation that checks the routed department against the actual ticket content.

examples.title: Recovering a Reasoning Scratchpad Inside a Constrained Schema
examples.explanation: Schema A is not wrong or broken -- it will reliably produce a syntactically valid integer -- but on anything harder than a lookup, it forces the model to commit to a final number as close to immediately as the schema allows, with no intermediate tokens to build on, which is exactly the scenario the next-token-prediction module identified as hurting accuracy on multi-step problems. Schema B recovers that lost scratchpad without giving up any of the reliability benefit of constrained decoding: `reasoning` and `answer` are both still guaranteed-valid fields in a guaranteed-valid object, but because JSON object keys are emitted in the order the schema (and, practically, most implementations) lay them out, the `answer` field's tokens are generated after -- and conditioned on -- whatever the model wrote in `reasoning`. This is a genuinely important, easy-to-miss schema design lever: field order inside the object is not just cosmetic, it directly shapes what each field's value gets to condition on.

misconceptions.description: Once a response comes back through a genuine schema-constrained/structured-output feature, it's guaranteed correct and doesn't need any further validation before being used.
misconceptions.clarification: Schema constraints guarantee syntactic validity and structural conformance -- the right keys, the right types -- but say nothing at all about whether the values are true, sensible, or appropriate for the specific input. A model can be forced to emit a syntactically perfect but entirely fabricated value (a wrong year, a hallucinated ID, an enum choice from a set that didn't actually contain the correct option), because the underlying generation mechanism -- and its capacity for hallucination -- operates completely underneath the constraint layer. Production code should still validate values against business rules and, for consequential decisions, treat the output as a claim to verify rather than a guaranteed fact.

misconceptions.description: Schema-constrained decoding makes the model better at the underlying task, not just more consistently formatted.
misconceptions.clarification: The constraint only restricts which tokens are eligible for selection at each step -- it has no effect on the quality of the model's underlying reasoning or knowledge, and it can actively hurt task performance if the schema forces a final answer immediately with no room for intermediate reasoning tokens to condition on. A schema that jumps straight to a rigid answer field can measurably reduce accuracy on harder problems compared to letting the model reason freely first; the fix is to design the schema to include a reasoning field ordered before the answer, not to expect the constraint itself to make the model more capable.

exercises.prompt: A ticket-routing schema declares `"priority": {"enum": ["low", "medium", "high"]}` as a required field, with strict schema-constrained decoding enabled. A genuinely urgent, safety-related ticket comes in that arguably deserves a priority level above all three declared options (something like 'critical' or 'emergency'). What will the model's structured output actually contain for the `priority` field, and why?
exercises.code:
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"priority": {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high"]}},
    "required": ["priority"],
    "additionalProperties": False
}

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Classify priority: 'Gas leak reported in the building, evacuate immediately.'"}],
    response_format={"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "routing", "schema": schema, "strict": True}},
)
hints: Constrained decoding zeroes out the probability of any token that isn't part of an allowed continuation under the schema -- what tokens are even eligible for the value of `priority` here?
The model cannot invent a fourth option or leave the field blank if it's required and the enum only lists three values -- what does it do instead?
Think about which of the three declared options is the closest, most plausible-sounding fallback for something this urgent, even though none of them technically fits.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The output will still be valid JSON with `priority` set to one of the three declared enum values -- almost certainly "high", as the closest available option -- because the decoder is mechanically incapable of emitting anything outside the enum, including a more appropriate label the schema author never anticipated. The schema constraint guarantees a syntactically valid answer, not a correct or sufficiently expressive one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because `priority` is both required and constrained to an enum of exactly three values, every token position for that field's value has its eligible token set restricted to sequences forming one of "low", "medium", or "high" -- there is no path through the constrained decoding process that could ever produce "critical" or "emergency", regardless of how strongly the model's unconstrained preferences might favor a stronger label for a genuinely life-threatening situation. The model will pick the closest available option, most likely "high", and the resulting JSON will pass schema validation perfectly -- which is exactly the danger: a downstream system checking only 'is this valid according to the schema' has no way to detect that the enum itself was too narrow for this input. This is a direct illustration of why schema design -- including deliberately providing headroom for genuinely extreme cases -- matters as much as remembering to turn constrained decoding on in the first place.

exercises.prompt: A team built a schema-constrained extractor for solving word problems that returns just a final numeric answer, and accuracy on multi-step arithmetic word problems is noticeably worse than the same model answering in plain, unconstrained text. Diagnose why constraining the output could plausibly cause this regression, and fix the schema without giving up structured output.
hints: Generation is strictly left-to-right -- with only one field in the schema, what is the very first thing the model is forced to generate, and what does it have to condition on at that point?
Compare this to the unconstrained plain-text version, which presumably wrote out some reasoning before stating a final number -- where did that reasoning go in the constrained version?
Consider adding a field to the schema, ordered so it comes before `answer`, that gives the model somewhere to work through the problem before committing to the number.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original schema has exactly one required field, `answer`, so the very first tokens the model is permitted to generate are already part of the final numeric answer -- there is no space anywhere in the constrained output for the kind of intermediate step-by-step reasoning that a plain-text response was free to include before stating its conclusion. This directly removes the accuracy benefit that explicit intermediate reasoning provides on multi-step problems, covered in the next-token-prediction module: the model has to jump straight from the question to a committed number with nothing in between to condition on. Adding a `reasoning` field, ordered before `answer` in the schema, restores that scratchpad entirely within the constrained, schema-valid structure -- the model writes out its reasoning first (still perfectly valid JSON), and the `answer` field's tokens are then generated conditioned on that reasoning text, recovering most of the accuracy of unconstrained chain-of-thought while keeping the hard reliability guarantee of a parseable, correctly-typed final answer.

assessments.prompt: What is the key mechanical difference between instructing a model to 'return valid JSON' in plain text versus using a genuine schema-constrained decoding feature?
options: There is no real difference -- both rely on the model choosing to follow the instruction, and structured-output features are just a more politely-worded version of the same request.

The plain-text instruction only shapes the probability distribution over likely next tokens; the schema-constrained feature actively zeroes out the probability of any token that would violate the schema before a token is even selected, making invalid tokens impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Schema-constrained decoding works by running the model's output through a separate validator after generation and re-generating from scratch if it fails, rather than changing anything about generation itself.
Schema-constrained decoding guarantees both syntactic validity and that every field's value is factually correct, since the schema defines exactly what's allowed.
assessments.explanation: The defining mechanism is the token-masking step applied before softmax: logits for any token that would break the schema are forced to negative infinity, so those tokens have exactly zero probability of selection -- a fundamentally stronger guarantee than an instruction, which only shifts probabilities without eliminating any option outright. Option A wrongly treats structured-output features as just a stronger-worded instruction. Option C misdescribes the mechanism as after-the-fact validation and regeneration, when it actually operates during generation, at each decoding step. Option D overstates the guarantee -- schema constraints ensure syntactic and structural validity, never factual correctness of the values themselves.

assessments.prompt: Explain why forcing a model's output directly into a rigid final-answer schema can sometimes make its answers less accurate, not just differently formatted, and how a schema can be redesigned to avoid that cost.
assessments.modelAnswer: Generation is strictly autoregressive and left-to-right: every token is produced conditioned only on the tokens that already exist in the sequence, with no separate planning phase and no way to revise something already committed. When a schema's only field is the final answer itself, the very first tokens the model is permitted to generate under that constraint are already part of that committed answer -- there is no room anywhere in the output for the kind of intermediate reasoning tokens (working through sub-steps, restating relevant facts, computing intermediate quantities) that measurably improve accuracy on harder, multi-step problems, because those techniques work precisely by giving the model real generated text to condition later tokens on rather than forcing a jump straight from question to answer. A rigid single-field schema recreates exactly that forced jump, just wrapped in valid JSON syntax instead of plain text, so whatever accuracy loss comes from skipping explicit intermediate reasoning shows up here too, on top of -- and unrelated to -- the schema's formatting benefit. The fix does not require giving up structured output: adding an additional field, such as `reasoning`, and ordering it *before* the final answer field within the same JSON object, lets the model generate its reasoning first while still inside a fully schema-valid structure; because JSON object fields are emitted in the order the schema specifies, the answer field's tokens are then generated conditioned on whatever reasoning text came before them, recovering most of the benefit of an unconstrained chain-of-thought response without sacrificing the hard guarantee that the output will parse and match the required shape. The general lesson is that a schema is not just a passive description of the desired shape of the output -- its field order actively shapes what each field's value gets to condition on, and that's a design lever worth using deliberately rather than an accident of how you happened to list the fields.

concepts.title: Function Calling: How Models Invoke Tools
concepts.description: Function calling is schema-constrained generation aimed at a specific purpose: the model produces a structured description of which function it wants called and with what arguments, but it never executes anything itself -- your application code decides whether to actually run that function, runs it, and feeds the real result back into the conversation for the model to continue from.
learningObjectives: Explain the full tool-calling request/response cycle: tool definitions, the model's structured call request, application-side execution, and feeding the result back in.
Explain why the model never executes a function itself, and what that implies for validating arguments before running consequential code.
Describe how a model 'decides' to call a tool versus respond directly, in terms of the next-token-prediction mechanism, and why tool descriptions function as prompt engineering.
Design tool definitions -- name, description, and parameter schema -- that reliably elicit correct tool selection and well-formed arguments.
Diagnose and fix common tool-calling bugs: wrong tool selected, hallucinated arguments, and results that never get fed back into the conversation.

sections.heading: The Tool-Calling Cycle, Stage by Stage
How the Model 'Decides' to Call a Tool
sections.body:
It's worth being precise about what 'decides' means here, because it's easy to accidentally imagine a symbolic reasoning step evaluating whether a tool is logically necessary. There is no such step. Whether the model emits ordinary text or a tool-call request at a given turn is itself just the outcome of next-token prediction -- during training, the model has learned an association between certain conditioning patterns (a system message listing available tools, a user request whose phrasing resembles ones that were paired with tool use during training) and a higher probability of the next tokens forming a tool-call structure rather than ordinary prose.

This has two very practical consequences. First, **a tool's name and description function exactly like a piece of prompt engineering**, because they are quite literally additional conditioning text sent to the model on every call -- an ambiguous or generic description (`"search"`, described only as "searches for things") gives the model far less signal to correctly decide when this specific tool, rather than some other similarly-named one, is the right choice, in exactly the way a vague prompt produces inconsistent behavior. Second, this explains both directions of tool-selection failure: a model can call a tool unnecessarily (its description sounded superficially relevant to a request that didn't actually need it) or fail to call a genuinely necessary tool (its description didn't use language that resembled the user's phrasing closely enough to raise the probability of a tool-call token sequence). Neither failure means the model 'misunderstood' the task in a deliberative sense -- both are the direct, mechanical result of how conditioning text shapes a probability distribution, which is exactly why improving tool descriptions is usually a far more effective fix than trying to make the underlying instruction more emphatic.

sections.heading: Argument Hallucination, and Why Validation Before Execution Is Mandatory
Feeding Results Back: Context Growth and What Not to Dump In
sections.body:
The tool's real result gets appended to the conversation as a new message (commonly given a dedicated role, like `"tool"`), and the model is called again with that result now part of what it conditions on. This is the same context-window mechanics from the tokenization module applied to a new source of content: every tool result you feed back in consumes real tokens from the same shared budget as everything else, and a multi-tool conversation grows with every round trip, exactly the way an unmanaged chat history does.

A common, avoidable mistake is feeding an entire raw API response or database row set back into the conversation just because it was convenient to pass through unmodified -- a bulky JSON blob with dozens of irrelevant fields not only wastes tokens and money, it also reintroduces the 'lost in the middle' risk from earlier: the one field the model actually needs from that result can get buried among many it doesn't, weakening the model's ability to use it correctly in its next response. The better default is to have your tool-execution code shape the result down to what's actually relevant before appending it -- extracting the specific fields needed rather than passing the full raw payload through untouched -- the same discipline as curating retrieved context in a RAG pipeline, applied here to tool output instead of retrieved documents.

examples.title: The Full Tool-Calling Loop, End to End
examples.code:
def get_order_status(order_id):
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "eta_days": 2}   # a real lookup, in practice

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Where's my order ORD-48213?"}]

response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
tool_call = response.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0]
args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)

result = get_order_status(args["order_id"])   # YOUR code actually runs the lookup

messages.append(response.choices[0].message)
messages.append({
    "role": "tool",
    "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
    "content": json.dumps(result)
})

final = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
print(final.choices[0].message.content)
# "Your order ORD-48213 has shipped and is expected in 2 days."
examples.explanation: Notice exactly where real execution happens: `get_order_status(args["order_id"])` is ordinary application code, called explicitly by this script, not something the model triggered directly or ran inside itself. The model's only contribution at the first step is the structured request -- name plus arguments -- and its only contribution at the second step is turning the real result, now sitting in the conversation as a tool message, into a natural-language answer. Both `response.choices[0].message` (the assistant's tool-call request) and the new `"tool"` message need to be appended to `messages` before the second call, or the model calling a second time would have no idea a tool was ever invoked or what it returned -- omitting either line is exactly the kind of structural bug covered in the debugging exercise below.

examples.title: Argument Hallucination: A Schema-Valid but Fabricated User ID
examples.code:
# Conversation never states a user ID explicitly -- it's implied by session context,
# which the model can't see unless it's actually included in the prompt.
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You can cancel subscriptions using the cancel_subscription tool."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Please cancel my subscription."}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=cancel_tools)
tool_call = response.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0]
print(tool_call.function.arguments)
# e.g. '{"user_id": "usr_1001"}'  -- a schema-valid but ENTIRELY FABRICATED user ID,
# since no user ID was ever actually given anywhere in this conversation.
examples.explanation: The tool call is perfectly well-formed: valid JSON, correct field name, correct type -- and the value is fiction. The model was never given the real authenticated user's ID anywhere in the messages it conditioned on, so `"user_id"` in its output is simply whatever the schema-constrained decoder produced as a plausible-looking string for a required field it had no actual grounding for, the exact same mechanism as any other hallucination. Code that executed this tool call directly, trusting the argument at face value, would risk cancelling the wrong account entirely. The fix is architectural, not a better prompt: sensitive identifiers like the acting user's ID should come from your application's own trusted session state at execution time, never be accepted as-is from the model's generated arguments for a destructive action.

examples.title: Tool Descriptions Are Prompting: Fixing Ambiguous Routing Between Two Tools
examples.code:
# Vague: both descriptions sound similar, so tool selection is inconsistent
vague_tools = [
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "search_docs", "description": "Searches for information.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}}},
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "search_web", "description": "Searches for information.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}}},
]

# Specific: each description marks a clearly different, non-overlapping use case
clear_tools = [
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "search_docs", "description": "Searches ONLY this company's internal product documentation and policy pages. Use for questions about our own product, pricing, or policies.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}}},
    {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "search_web", "description": "Searches the public internet for general, current information NOT related to this company's own product or policies.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}}},
]
examples.explanation: With the vague descriptions, both tools condition the model almost identically -- 'searches for information' gives the model essentially no basis to prefer one over the other, so tool selection for a query like 'what's your refund policy?' can go either way inconsistently across calls, exactly like the vague-prompt problem from the earlier prompting module. The clear descriptions each stake out a distinct, mutually exclusive territory in plain language, which sharpens which tool's name becomes the higher-probability continuation for a given query -- a policy question now conditions much more strongly toward `search_docs`, and a general current-events question toward `search_web`. Nothing about the tools' actual implementations changed between the two versions; only the conditioning text describing them did, which is exactly the point -- tool descriptions are prompt-engineering surface area, not documentation that the model consults separately from the rest of the prompt.

misconceptions.description: When a model returns a tool call, it has actually executed that function itself, inside its own process, and the returned content is the real result.
misconceptions.clarification: A tool call is only ever a structured text request -- a name and a JSON object of arguments -- generated by the same token-by-token mechanism as any other output. The model has no ability to reach out and run code, query a database, or call an API on its own; every real execution step happens entirely in your application code, which decides whether to run the requested function at all, runs it for real, and is responsible for feeding the actual result back in. This has direct security implications: since your code is the only thing standing between a tool-call request and real-world execution, it is also the only place where validation, authorization, and safety checks can happen.

misconceptions.description: If a tool call's arguments are schema-valid and well-typed, the values inside them can be trusted and executed directly.
misconceptions.clarification: Schema validity guarantees the arguments parse and match the declared types -- it says nothing about whether the values are grounded in anything real. A model can generate a perfectly well-formed but entirely fabricated argument (an invented ID, a guessed date, a plausible-looking value for a field the conversation never actually specified), through the exact same hallucination mechanism that produces fabricated facts in plain text. Any argument feeding into a consequential or side-effecting action should be validated against your application's own trusted state -- session data, database lookups, authorization checks -- before it's ever executed, not accepted at face value because it happened to arrive as clean JSON.

exercises.prompt: This tool-calling loop executes the requested function correctly but the model's final response always sounds like it never actually saw the tool's result -- it responds generically instead of using the real order status. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
def handle_message(user_text, client, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}]
    response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
    tool_call = response.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0]
    args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
    result = get_order_status(args["order_id"])

    final = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
    return final.choices[0].message.content
hints: Compare `messages` right before the second API call to what it was before the first call -- has anything actually been added to it?

The assistant's tool-call request and the tool's real result both need to become part of the conversation history before calling the model again, or the second call has no way to know a tool was ever invoked.
Two `.append()` calls are missing: one for the assistant's tool-call message, one for a `"tool"`-role message containing `result`.
exercises.solutionCode:
def handle_message(user_text, client, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}]
    response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
    tool_call = response.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0]
    args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
    result = get_order_status(args["order_id"])

    messages.append(response.choices[0].message)
    messages.append({
        "role": "tool",
        "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
        "content": json.dumps(result)
    })

    final = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
    return final.choices[0].message.content
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is structurally identical to the RAG augmentation bug from the earlier module -- a value (there, retrieved context; here, the tool's result) is correctly computed but never actually included in what gets sent to the model. The second `client.chat.completions.create` call reuses the exact same `messages` list from before the tool call happened, with neither the assistant's tool-call request nor the tool's real result ever appended to it -- so from the model's point of view, the second call looks identical to the first, and it has no way to know a tool was invoked or what it returned. The fix appends both the assistant's tool-call message and a new `"tool"`-role message carrying the real result before calling the model again, which is what actually lets the second call condition on, and respond using, the genuine data.

exercises.prompt: Write a function `execute_tool_call(tool_call, session)` for a `"cancel_subscription"` tool that takes a `user_id` argument. It must parse the tool call's JSON arguments, and if the tool name is `"cancel_subscription"`, it must NOT trust the model-provided `user_id` for execution -- instead it should verify that the provided `user_id` matches `session.authenticated_user_id`, raise a `PermissionError` if they don't match, and otherwise call `cancel_subscription(session.authenticated_user_id)` and return its result. Raise `ValueError` for any other tool name.
hints: Parse `tool_call.function.arguments` with `json.loads` first -- it's a JSON string, not already a dict.
The check should compare the model's claimed `user_id` against `session.authenticated_user_id` -- if they differ, raise PermissionError rather than proceeding.
Even after the check passes, execute using `session.authenticated_user_id` (the trusted value), not the argument the model supplied, as the actual source of truth.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The key design decision is that the model-supplied `user_id` is used only as something to check, never as something to act on directly -- `session.authenticated_user_id`, a value your application already trusts independent of anything the model generated, is what actually gets passed to `cancel_subscription`. If the two don't match, the function refuses the action outright rather than proceeding with a warning or a best guess, because there's no safe way to partially trust a hallucinated identifier on a destructive action. This pattern generalizes: for any tool that changes real state, the model's arguments should be treated as a proposed action to validate against ground truth your code controls, not as ground truth themselves.

assessments.prompt: When an LLM API response includes a tool call, what has actually happened at that point?
options: The model has already executed the corresponding function internally, and the tool call is just a log of what it did.
The model has generated a structured request -- a tool name and JSON arguments -- and no real function has been executed yet; the calling application must parse this request and choose to execute it.
The API provider's infrastructure has automatically executed the function on the model's behalf before returning the response.
The tool call is only a suggestion; the model will execute the real function on the next turn regardless of what the application does.
assessments.explanation: A tool call is generated content, produced by the same underlying next-token mechanism as any other output, constrained to match the tool's declared schema -- it is a request for your application to act on, not evidence that any real execution has occurred. Option A and option C both wrongly locate execution inside the model or the provider's infrastructure, when execution is entirely the calling application's responsibility. Option D is wrong because nothing happens automatically on 'the next turn' -- if the application never executes the function and never feeds a result back, the model has no way to know whether anything happened at all.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'Our tool calls always come back as perfectly valid, correctly-typed JSON, so I don't see why we need extra validation before running them.' Explain what's wrong with this reasoning, tying it back to how tool-calling arguments are actually generated, and describe the validation discipline you'd put in place instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Schema-constrained decoding, which is what makes tool-call arguments reliably well-formed, only restricts which tokens are eligible for selection at each generation step -- it guarantees the resulting JSON will parse and that each field will have the declared type, but it has no mechanism for checking whether the values inside it are actually true or appropriate for the current situation. The arguments are still produced by the same probabilistic, next-token generation process that produces every other piece of model output, including its capacity to hallucinate: a `user_id`, an order number, a file path, or a date can all be syntactically perfect and still be entirely fabricated, especially if the conversation never actually supplied the real value and the model filled in something plausible-sounding to satisfy a required field. Treating 'this parsed successfully' as equivalent to 'this is safe to execute' conflates two completely different guarantees. The validation discipline I'd put in place is to treat every tool-call argument as an untrusted claim proposed by the model, with the strength of validation scaled to the consequence of the action: read-only, low-stakes tools (a calculator, a public lookup) can reasonably execute with light or no additional validation, but anything that changes real state -- cancelling something, sending a communication, moving money, deleting a resource -- needs its consequential arguments checked against ground truth the application already controls, such as the actual authenticated session, a database record, or an explicit business rule, before execution proceeds; a mismatch should hard-fail rather than proceed with a best guess. This mirrors exactly how plain hallucinated prose needs grounding or verification before being trusted for anything consequential -- tool arguments just make the risk easier to overlook because the output happens to look clean and machine-generated rather than obviously prose-like.

concepts.title: Agentic Loops: Plan, Act, Observe
concepts.description: An agent is a tool-calling cycle that simply doesn't stop after one round: the model repeatedly decides whether to call another tool or produce a final answer, conditioning each decision on the accumulating record of its own prior actions and their real observed results, until it signals it's done or an external safety limit stops it.
learningObjectives: Describe the plan-act-observe loop and map each phase onto the tool-calling mechanism from the previous concept.
Explain why an agentic loop is an incremental extension of single-round tool calling rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and why its 'planning' is still ordinary generated text.
Identify failure modes specific to multi-step loops: compounding errors, repetitive/stuck loops, runaway cost, and unbounded context growth.
Design concrete guardrails for an agent loop: iteration caps, cost budgets, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-stakes actions.
Explain why an agent's tool-based self-checks reduce but do not eliminate compounding-error risk.

sections.heading: From One Tool Call to a Loop
sections.body:
The previous concept's tool-calling cycle ended, deliberately, after a single round: request, execute, feed the result back, get a final answer. An agentic loop is exactly that same cycle, run repeatedly, without assuming the model is done after one tool result comes back. After the tool result is appended to the conversation and the model is called again, instead of necessarily producing a final text answer, the model may generate *another* tool-call request -- and your orchestration code executes that one too, appends its result, and calls the model again, and so on.

```python
def run_agent(user_text, client, tools, tool_functions, max_iterations=8):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}]
    for _ in range(max_iterations):
        response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", messages=messages, tools=tools)
        message = response.choices[0].message
        messages.append(message)
        if not message.tool_calls:
            return message.content   # model chose to respond directly -- loop ends
        for tool_call in message.tool_calls:
            args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
            result = tool_functions[tool_call.function.name](**args)
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": tool_call.id, "content": json.dumps(result)})
    return "Stopped: reached max_iterations without a final answer."
```

It's worth stating plainly what has and hasn't changed relative to the previous concept: nothing about the underlying mechanism is new. There is no additional module, no separate agent 'brain' bolted on -- it is the identical request/execute/feed-back cycle, wrapped in a `for` loop that keeps going until the model produces plain text instead of a tool call, or until an external limit (like `max_iterations` above) cuts it off. Everything interesting and everything risky about agentic behavior follows directly from running that familiar cycle more than once in a row.

sections.heading: 'Plan, Act, Observe' Describes the Loop -- It Isn't a Separate Module
sections.body:
The pattern is often named explicitly in the literature and in agent frameworks as **ReAct** (reason plus act): at each iteration, the model may generate some explicit reasoning text (often literally prefixed 'Thought:' in older implementations, or just ordinary prose preceding a tool call in modern ones), then an action (the tool call itself), and then, once your code executes it, an observation (the real tool result, fed back into context) -- which becomes input to the next iteration's reasoning, and the cycle repeats.

It's essential to carry over a lesson from the how-LLMs-work module here rather than quietly abandoning it just because the word 'planning' is now in the air: text that reads as a plan -- 'I'll first look up the customer's order, then check the refund policy, then decide' -- is still ordinary generated output, produced by the exact same next-token-prediction mechanism as everything else, conditioned only on what's in the context so far. It is not evidence of a persistent, symbolic planning module tracking progress toward a goal across iterations. Whatever looks like sustained, goal-directed deliberation across many steps is actually the model regenerating its 'plan' fresh, from scratch, at every single iteration, conditioned on the entire growing transcript of everything it and the tools have said and done so far -- the appearance of continuity comes entirely from that transcript being resent every time, not from any internal state the model carries between calls.

sections.heading: Compounding Errors and Loops That Don't Converge
sections.body:
The previous concept's argument-hallucination risk doesn't go away in a multi-step loop -- it compounds. An error introduced at step 2 (a wrong tool chosen, a hallucinated argument, a misread observation) becomes a permanent part of the context that every subsequent step conditions on, for exactly the reason the how-LLMs-work module described for plain generation: there is no built-in mechanism that revisits or re-evaluates an earlier commitment, so later steps tend to build fluently *on top of* an earlier mistake rather than catching it.

A distinctive multi-step failure mode worth naming specifically is an agent **misreading an unhelpful or error-bearing tool result as success** and proceeding down a wrong path for several more steps before anything visibly goes wrong -- for instance, a tool call that returns an empty result set or an error string formatted similarly to real data, which the model then treats as a valid (if sparse) answer and reasons forward from, compounding the original misunderstanding across every remaining iteration. A related, more mechanical failure is an agent getting **stuck oscillating between two unproductive actions** -- retrying the same failing tool call with slightly different arguments repeatedly, or alternating between two tools that don't actually make progress on the task -- which, left unchecked, simply consumes iterations, tokens, and money without ever reaching a real answer. Neither failure is rare or exotic; both are direct, expected consequences of a loop with no built-in convergence guarantee and no automatic mechanism for detecting that it isn't making progress.

sections.heading: Guardrails: Iteration Caps, Cost Budgets, and Human Checkpoints
sections.body:
None of the failure modes above are prevented by the base mechanism -- they have to be engineered in deliberately, the same way hallucination mitigation had to be engineered in for plain generation. A **hard iteration cap** (the `max_iterations` parameter above) is the minimum viable guardrail: it converts an unbounded, potentially runaway loop into one with a known worst-case cost and a known worst-case latency, and an agent that hits the cap without finishing should report that failure explicitly rather than silently returning its last, possibly-wrong intermediate state as if it were a final answer.

A **cost or token budget**, tracked across the whole run rather than per call, catches a different failure shape -- a loop that's technically making some progress each round but is far more expensive than the task warrants, which an iteration cap alone won't necessarily catch if each individual iteration looks reasonable. Requiring the model to signal completion through an **explicit 'finish' or 'submit_answer' tool**, rather than inferring completion from the absence of a tool call, gives you a single, unambiguous, loggable event marking task completion, rather than relying on an implicit signal that's easy to mishandle in orchestration code. And for any tool in the agent's toolkit that performs a **side-effecting or hard-to-reverse action** -- sending an email, executing a payment, deleting a resource -- a human-approval checkpoint before that specific tool actually executes is a categorically different kind of safeguard than any of the others: it directly addresses the fact that a multi-step agent can now chain together several consequential tool calls autonomously, compounding the single-call argument-hallucination risk from the previous concept across an entire unsupervised sequence of actions before a human ever sees any of them. Logging every step -- every tool call, every argument, every raw result -- as the run happens is what makes any of this debuggable after the fact; a failed multi-step run with no step-by-step record is close to unfixable.

sections.heading: What an Agentic Loop Isn't
sections.body: It's worth closing on a deliberate note of restraint, because the term 'agent' invites overclaiming. Popular agent frameworks add real scaffolding on top of this loop -- structured memory stores, multiple cooperating model calls playing different roles, more sophisticated stopping criteria -- but none of that scaffolding changes the fundamental mechanism described here: every individual decision inside any of these systems is still a next-token-prediction step, conditioned on whatever text has been assembled into context, with no persistent internal cognition, no ground-truth self-awareness of whether it's actually making progress, and no guarantee of convergence. An agent 'checking its own work' by calling a verification tool is a genuinely useful and common mitigation, and it does reduce the practical rate of compounding errors -- but it works by adding more of the same mechanism (another tool call, another generated interpretation of its result), not by introducing a fundamentally more reliable one, and it inherits the exact same risk of being itself misread or skipped that motivated using it in the first place.

examples.title: A Minimal Agent Loop With an Iteration Guard
examples.explanation: The loop's exit conditions are exactly the two described in the explanation: the model responding without any tool call (a genuine, self-signaled completion, handled in the `if not message.tool_calls` branch), and the iteration cap being reached with no such signal (handled by the `for` loop simply running out and falling through to the `max_iterations_reached` result). Returning an explicit status dict rather than just a string is a small but meaningful design choice -- it makes the difference between 'the agent finished' and 'the agent was cut off' visible and checkable to calling code, rather than silently returning `None` or an empty string in the failure case, which would be easy to mistake for a genuine (if unhelpful) answer.

examples.title: A Misread Observation Compounds Into a Wrong Answer
examples.code:
# Step 2: agent calls a lookup tool for a customer's order
tool_result = {"error": "No order found matching that ID."}
messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": json.dumps(tool_result)})

# Step 3: model conditions on that result -- if it misreads the error-shaped dict
# as though it were sparse-but-valid order data rather than an explicit failure...
# next_response.choices[0].message.content might become something like:
# "Your order has no items associated with it -- there may have been a processing issue."
# ...continuing to build a plausible-sounding narrative on top of a result that
# actually meant "the lookup failed," not "the order exists and happens to be empty."
examples.explanation: The tool executed correctly and returned an honest, well-formed error -- the bug is entirely in how the next generation step interprets that observation. Because `{"error": "No order found..."}` is still just JSON text appended into context, the model has to infer its meaning the same way it infers meaning from anything else in the conversation, and nothing in the base mechanism guarantees it will correctly distinguish 'this is a failure signal' from 'this is unusual-but-real data.' Once it settles on the wrong interpretation, every subsequent sentence is generated to be a fluent, locally coherent continuation of that wrong premise, exactly as the how-LLMs-work module described for a single wrong token -- except now the 'wrong token' is an entire misread tool result, and the compounding plays out across however many remaining iterations build on it. A concrete mitigation is to design tool results with an explicit, unambiguous, consistently-named status field (`{"ok": false, "reason": "not_found"}`) and instruct the model explicitly on how to handle that shape, rather than relying on it to infer failure from a loosely-structured error message.

examples.title: A Human Checkpoint Before a Destructive Tool Executes
examples.explanation: This checkpoint is a categorically different kind of guardrail than an iteration cap or a cost budget -- it doesn't just bound how much a runaway loop can cost, it inserts a human decision directly into the causal path of any tool call that could cause real, hard-to-reverse harm, regardless of how many iterations the agent has run or how much budget remains. `DESTRUCTIVE_TOOLS` is deliberately an explicit allowlist-style check rather than something inferred from the tool's behavior at runtime, because tool names and their consequences should be known and classified ahead of time by whoever designs the agent's toolkit, not discovered empirically after something goes wrong. Everything upstream of this function -- tool selection, argument generation, however many prior loop iterations led here -- can be exactly as autonomous as the rest of the agent; the checkpoint's entire job is to make sure autonomy stops at the specific boundary where an action becomes consequential enough to need a second, human check.

misconceptions.description: An agentic loop means the model has a persistent internal planning process that tracks progress toward the overall goal across iterations, the way a person keeps a mental plan in mind while working through a task.
misconceptions.clarification: There is no persistent internal state carried between iterations beyond whatever text has been appended to the growing message list -- each iteration, the model regenerates its 'reasoning' and next action completely fresh, conditioned only on that accumulated transcript, with no memory of having 'decided' anything except insofar as that decision was written down as text and resent. The appearance of sustained, goal-directed planning is entirely a byproduct of the orchestration code resending the full history every time, not evidence of an internal agent state persisting inside the model between calls.

misconceptions.description: Because an agent can use tools to check its own work -- calling a calculator to verify a computed number, or re-querying a database to confirm a claim -- it will reliably catch its own mistakes before finishing.
misconceptions.clarification: A self-check tool call only helps if the model both decides to make it and correctly interprets its result -- neither is guaranteed, since both are themselves ordinary generation steps subject to the same failure modes as everything else: the model might skip the check entirely, misread an ambiguous or error-shaped result as confirming rather than contradicting its prior step, or run the check against the wrong thing. Self-verification meaningfully reduces the rate of compounding errors in practice and is worth building in deliberately, but it is an added mitigation layered on top of the same mechanism, not a different, more reliable one -- it inherits the exact same risks of misinterpretation that motivated adding it.

exercises.prompt: This agent loop occasionally runs for a very long time and racks up unexpectedly high API costs on certain inputs, because the model keeps calling a lookup tool that returns an unhelpful or empty result, retrying with slightly different arguments each time, without ever concluding. Find the missing guardrail and fix it.
hints: The loop's only exit condition is the model eventually responding without a tool call -- what happens if that never occurs, for instance because the model keeps retrying an unhelpful tool instead of giving up?
There is no cap anywhere on how many times this `while True` loop can execute -- add one.
A capped loop needs an explicit fallback return for the case where the cap is reached without the model ever producing a final answer, rather than looping forever.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `while True` has exactly one way out -- the model eventually responding with plain text instead of a tool call -- and nothing in the base mechanism guarantees that will happen within any bounded number of steps, especially when a tool keeps returning unhelpful results that the model interprets as worth retrying with different arguments rather than as a reason to stop. Replacing `while True` with `for _ in range(max_iterations)` gives the loop a hard, known worst-case bound on both cost and latency, and the added fallback return after the loop makes the 'ran out of steps without finishing' outcome an explicit, visible result rather than an infinite hang -- which is exactly the minimum guardrail every agent loop needs before it's safe to run on inputs you don't fully control in advance.

exercises.prompt: An agent's lookup tool returns `{"error": "rate limited, try again later"}` at step 3 of a run. The agent has no special handling for error-shaped tool results and no self-verification step. Predict what the agent is likely to do at step 4, and explain why, based on how tool results feed back into generation.
exercises.code:
# Step 3 tool result, appended into the conversation as-is:
messages.append({
    "role": "tool",
    "tool_call_id": "call_3",
    "content": json.dumps({"error": "rate limited, try again later"})
})

# Step 4: model is called again with this in context. What is the most
# likely category of response, given no special error-handling instructions
# exist anywhere in the system prompt or tool descriptions?
hints: The model has to generate SOME plausible continuation at step 4 -- there's no built-in 'pause and wait' behavior unless it's explicitly engineered in.

Consider the range of plausible next actions: retrying the same tool immediately, treating the error message as if it were real (if oddly-shaped) data, or giving up and answering without the needed information -- none of which are reliably the 'correct' choice without explicit guidance.

The point isn't to predict the exact wording -- it's to recognize that the outcome is unreliable and underspecified precisely because no instruction anywhere tells the model what a rate-limit error actually means it should do.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Without explicit error-handling instructions, the agent's behavior at step 4 is genuinely underdetermined and can go several plausible-but-inconsistent ways across repeated runs: it might immediately retry the same tool call (a reasonable-sounding but potentially wasteful reaction to 'try again later'), it might misinterpret the error dict as if it were sparse real data and proceed to answer based on it, or it might give up and answer the user's original question without the information it was trying to look up, possibly without flagging that anything went wrong. None of these is reliably the one that happens -- the underlying issue is that nothing in the prompt or tool description told the model how a rate-limit error specifically should be handled, so its response is whatever the training-derived default behavior for an ambiguous error-shaped observation happens to be.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A tool result, once appended to the conversation, is just more text the model conditions on -- exactly like any other observation -- and the model's next action is generated the same way any next-token sequence is generated: as a plausible continuation given everything currently in context, including whatever loosely-defined meaning it assigns to `{"error": "rate limited, try again later"}`. Because no system instruction or tool description in this scenario specifies how the agent should react to a rate-limit signal specifically (e.g. 'wait N seconds and retry once, then give up and inform the user'), the model has no strong, deliberately-shaped conditioning pushing it toward any one specific, reliable response -- it will produce something plausible-sounding, but which specific plausible response depends on subtle features of phrasing and can vary between runs. This is exactly why production agent designs treat error handling as something to specify explicitly, either in the tool's own description (documenting what error shapes mean and how to react) or in the system prompt, rather than trusting the model to infer sensible error-recovery behavior on its own from an ambiguous, unannotated result.

assessments.prompt: What actually changes, mechanically, when a single round of tool calling is extended into a full agentic loop?
options: The model gains a new, distinct planning module that tracks progress toward the goal across iterations, separate from its ordinary text generation.

Nothing new is introduced mechanically -- the same request/execute/feed-back-in tool-calling cycle is simply repeated by the orchestration code, conditioned each time on the growing transcript, until the model responds without a tool call or an external limit stops it.
The model begins executing tool code directly inside its own inference process once multiple tool calls are chained together.
The loop is guaranteed to converge to a correct final answer within a bounded number of steps, because each iteration narrows down the space of remaining possibilities.
assessments.explanation: An agentic loop is the same tool-calling mechanism from the previous concept, simply not stopped after one round -- your orchestration code keeps re-invoking the model with an ever-growing message history until a stopping condition is met. Option A wrongly attributes a persistent planning module to the model; any apparent planning is ordinary generated text, regenerated fresh each iteration from the full transcript. Option C misattributes execution to the model itself, when execution remains entirely the responsibility of the calling application at every iteration, exactly as in single-round tool calling. Option D is false and important to rule out explicitly -- there is no convergence guarantee at all; loops can stall, oscillate, or compound an early error indefinitely without an external cap, which is precisely why guardrails have to be engineered in rather than assumed.

assessments.prompt: A team is building an agent that can look up customer data and, when appropriate, issue refunds autonomously through a tool call. Explain, in terms of how the underlying loop actually works, why this design needs iteration caps, cost budgets, AND a human-approval checkpoint specifically before the refund tool executes -- and why none of the three alone would be sufficient.
assessments.modelAnswer: Each of the three guardrails addresses a different, independent way this loop can go wrong, and none of them substitutes for either of the others because they're not protecting against the same failure. An iteration cap protects against the loop simply never reaching a stopping condition -- because there's no built-in convergence guarantee, an agent can retry an ambiguous tool result, oscillate between two unproductive actions, or otherwise fail to make progress indefinitely unless something external forces it to stop after a bounded number of steps; but a capped loop can still run every one of those bounded iterations at real, nontrivial cost, which an iteration cap alone does nothing to control. A cost or token budget addresses that separate risk directly, catching a loop that is technically making progress each round but is disproportionately expensive relative to the task, a pattern an iteration cap won't necessarily flag if each individual step looks reasonable in isolation. Neither of those two guardrails, however, does anything about the qualitatively different risk introduced by including a refund tool at all: because tool-call arguments can be hallucinated -- schema-valid but not actually grounded in anything real, as covered when the mechanism was first introduced -- and because an agentic loop can chain several tool calls autonomously across many steps, a wrong or fabricated refund amount or target account could be executed as a side effect of an ordinary-looking multi-step run, with no human ever reviewing the specific action before it took effect financially. A human-approval checkpoint placed specifically in front of the refund tool's execution addresses exactly that gap, by inserting a review step at the one point where an error stops being a wasted API call and starts being real-world, hard-to-reverse harm -- and it needs to sit at that specific boundary regardless of how tightly the iteration count and cost budget are otherwise controlled, because a well-bounded, cheap loop can still autonomously execute one wrong refund just as easily as an unbounded one can.
